lessons.title: Hazrat Muhammad-ur-Rasool Ullah Khatam-un-Nabiyeen (S.A.W) — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
This unit tells us about Hazrat Muhammad-ur-Rasool Ullah Khatam-un-Nabiyeen (S.A.W), the last Rasool of Allah. Before Islam, the Arabs had indulged in all sorts of evils: they worshipped gods and goddesses instead of Almighty Allah, they gambled and drank wine, there was no respect for law, and nobody's life and property was safe.

Ameen and Sadiq

People called the Holy Prophet Ameen (the trustworthy) and Sadiq (the truthful) because of his honesty and truthfulness. The people of Makkah became his enemies because he asked them to worship the one and only Allah and to give up worshipping idols. They gave him a lot of trouble, but he faced all the hardships with courage and determination and kept on preaching the message of Allah.

The Journey to Madina

The journey from Makkah to Madina was very long and dangerous, because his enemies were looking for him everywhere and wanted to kill him. The Muslims of Madina were overjoyed to see him: many of them had already embraced Islam before he reached there, and Madina became the centre of Islam. Many Muslims of Makkah followed him to Madina to escape the painful treatment of the Kafirs.

What Islam Taught Mankind

  • Islam taught mankind to worship one Allah only, to fulfil their duties towards Allah and to serve their fellow men.
  • It taught honest rules of trade, encouraged people to seek knowledge, and gave a complete, practicable and successful way of life.
  • After the conquest of Makkah, the idols in the Kaaba were destroyed and the Arabs gave up gambling, drinking and fighting; nobody stole anything even if it was left by the roadside, and women got their due rights and respect.
  • The Holy Quran is the complete message of Allah; its light shows us the right path in every walk of life.

The unit's writing task is a unified paragraph on the importance of simplicity in life: a simple person lives within his means, avoids show and waste, and finds peace of mind, honesty, patience and gratitude in a simple life.

Key Points

  • Before Islam, the Arabs worshipped idols and had fallen into many evils.
  • The Holy Prophet was called Ameen and Sadiq for his honesty and truthfulness.
  • Madina became the centre of Islam after the Hijra.
  • Islam taught brotherhood, honesty and the worship of one Allah.

lessons.title: Unit 1 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 1 teaches kinds of nouns, gerunds and gerund phrases, and the kinds of sentences.

Kinds of Nouns

  • Collective noun — a group taken as one: council. The school council meets every Monday.
  • Countable noun — can be counted: photograph.
  • Uncountable noun — cannot be counted: information.
  • Material noun — a substance: diamond.
  • Abstract noun — a quality or idea: success. Hard work and patience are the keys to success.

Gerunds and Gerund Phrases

A gerund is the -ing form of a verb used as a noun: Smoking is injurious to health; Walking keeps man fit and healthy; Her writing has improved. A gerund phrase is a gerund with its words: eating ice cream on a hot day, studying for tests, jumping on the bed, riding a horse, working with computers.

Kinds of Sentences

  • Declarative (a statement): Hashim is my best friend.
  • Interrogative (a question): Where are you from?
  • Imperative (a command or request): Always obey your parents. Bring me a glass of water.
  • Exclamatory (strong feeling): What a tall man! Hurrah! We have won the match!

To change an affirmative sentence into an interrogative one, put the helping verb first: We should work for our country. → Should we work for our country? It is raining. → Is it raining?

Key Points

  • A gerund is a verb + -ing used as a noun.
  • There are four kinds of sentences: declarative, interrogative, imperative and exclamatory.
  • In a question, the helping verb comes before the subject.

mcqs.why: A gerund is the -ing form of a verb used as a noun, e.g. 'Smoking is injurious to health' and 'Walking keeps man fit.'

mcqs.why: A gerund phrase is a gerund with its words; 'eating ice cream on a hot day' is one of the unit's gerund phrases.

mcqs.q: 'Where are you from?' is which kind of sentence?
mcqs.why: A sentence that asks a question is interrogative; 'Where are you from?' asks a question.

mcqs.q: 'Always obey your parents' is which kind of sentence?
mcqs.why: An imperative sentence gives a command or request; 'Always obey your parents' is a command.

mcqs.why: An exclamatory sentence expresses strong feeling; 'Hurrah! We have won the match!' shows strong joy.

mcqs.q: How is 'It is raining' changed into an interrogative sentence?
mcqs.why: To change an affirmative sentence into a question, put the helping verb first: 'It is raining' becomes 'Is it raining?'

lessons.title: Science and Technology — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
The influence of modern technology can be seen in every walk of life. Scientific inventions have increased our happiness greatly: electricity and electronic machines have largely replaced manual labour and produce the necessaries of life in great abundance at a much lower cost.

Science in Our Daily Life

  • Our domestic life has become very comfortable with refrigerators, ovens, juicers, blenders, freezers and washing machines.
  • Fast means of travel and communication have made the world a global village: we can talk to friends thousands of miles away, and news travels within seconds by radio, television and social media.
  • In medical science, diseases once considered incurable can now be cured, and the transplantation of heart, liver and kidney has become possible.

Science in Education

Distance education offers flexible learning through online and print-based materials to students who cannot attend regular classes. The World Wide Web is one of the fastest media for teaching and learning, and computer conferencing lets students and teachers interact through e-mail, file transfer, chat rooms and real audio and video exchange.

The Dark Side of Science

The negative side of modern technology is the hydrogen bomb and the atom bomb. In August 1945, America dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in Japan, killing thousands of people. We should use modern discoveries and inventions for the welfare and betterment of humanity, not for destruction, chaos and uncertainty.

Key Points

  • Science has made domestic life comfortable and the world a global village.
  • Incurable diseases can now be cured; organ transplantation is possible.
  • Distance education and computer conferencing are new ways of learning.
  • The atom bomb is the dark side of science; inventions must serve humanity.

lessons.title: Unit 2 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 2 teaches adverbs in sentences and how to change the number of nouns.

Adverbs in Sentences

  • He always speaks honestly with his friends.
  • She reached school early in the morning.
  • The new mobile phone is quite expensive.
  • We visited our grandmother yesterday.
  • I have enough money to buy this book.
  • Sometimes I watch the news on television.

Changing the Number of Nouns

  • Most nouns add -s: stone → stones, photo → photos, piano → pianos, chief → chiefs.
  • Nouns ending in -ch add -es: stitch → stitches.
  • Consonant + y changes to -ies: lady → ladies.
  • -f changes to -ves: leaf → leaves.
  • Irregular plurals: goose → geese, man → men, foot → feet, child → children.
  • No change: deer → deer.
  • Compound nouns change their main word: daughter-in-law → daughters-in-law.

Key Points

  • Deer has the same singular and plural form.
  • Goose becomes geese and child becomes children.
  • Daughter-in-law becomes daughters-in-law.

lessons.title: The Wealthy Man — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
Naeem, a very rich man, had every luxury at his doorstep and could afford to feed all the people of his town. He boasted of his luxurious life to his friends and relatives. His friend Faheem, who lived in another city, came to spend his holidays with him.

The Visit to the Slum Area

Naeem took Faheem in his expensive car to the slum area of the town to show him how the poor lived. The slums were in a miserable condition: packs of stray dogs wandered here and there, trash heaps could be seen everywhere, there was no proper electricity or sanitation, and children were playing in unhygienic conditions, while at some distance people were ploughing and cultivating in the fields.

Faheem's Answer

  • You have only two dogs; they have ten dogs.
  • You have a big pool in your garden; they have a massive bay without any ends.
  • You have luxurious and expensive lights; they have countless stars lighting their nights.
  • You have a house on a small piece of land; they have abundant fields that go beyond the sight.
  • You are served by servants; they serve people.
  • You are protected by huge walls; they are tied with brotherhood and cooperation.

Naeem was stunned and speechless: Faheem's comparisons showed that the poor were richer than him in the real things of life — and that Naeem himself depended on them even for his food, which he bought from them.

The Moral of the Story

Real wealth is not money, luxury or property. True richness lies in contentment, brotherhood, cooperation, hard work and the blessings of nature. A person who boasts of his wealth is poor in spirit, while people who live simply and help one another are truly rich.

Key Points

  • Naeem boasted of his wealth and took Faheem to see the slums.
  • Faheem proved by comparisons that the poor were richer in real things.
  • The moral: real wealth is contentment and brotherhood, not money.

lessons.title: Unit 3 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 3 teaches phrases and clauses and how to rectify faulty punctuation.

Phrases and Clauses

A phrase is a group of words without a subject and a verb of its own: on the table, for a while, against all odds, as old as time. A clause has a subject and a verb. A main clause can stand alone as a sentence: We all will stand up. A subordinate clause depends on the main clause: When the president arrives, we all will stand up; She cried because her toy was broken. A relative clause begins with who, which or where and describes a noun: He is the teacher who has taught me in 8th class; This is the school where I study.

Punctuation

The book gives a passage with colons, question marks and apostrophes in the wrong places. Corrected, it reads with simple commas and full stops: "In the days of prosperity and pleasure, we sleep and enjoy and know not what we are. But in adversity, the inner man wakes up and we come to know our real strength and weakness." Remember: a statement ends with a full stop, not a question mark, and items in a flowing sentence are separated by commas.

Key Points

  • A phrase has no subject–verb pair; a clause has both.
  • A relative clause starts with who, which or where.
  • Wrong punctuation can change the whole meaning of a passage.

mcqs.q: What is a phrase?
options: A group of words without a subject and a verb of its own
A group of words with a subject and a verb
mcqs.why: A phrase is a group of words without a subject and a verb of its own, e.g. 'on the table' and 'for a while'.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a phrase?

mcqs.q: What is a clause?
options: A group of words with no verb

lessons.title: The Daffodils — The Poem in Simple Words
lessons.notes_html:
William Wordsworth was wandering lonely, like a cloud floating high over vales and hills, when suddenly he saw a host of golden daffodils beside the lake, beneath the trees, fluttering and dancing in the breeze. Daffodils are golden yellow flowers.

Stanza by Stanza

  • The daffodils were continuous as the stars that shine and twinkle on the Milky Way, stretched in a never-ending line along the margin of a bay. The poet saw ten thousand at a glance, tossing their heads in sprightly dance.
  • The waves beside them danced too, but the daffodils outdid the sparkling waves in glee. A poet could not but be gay in such a jocund company. The poet gazed and gazed, but little thought what wealth the show had brought him — here wealth means the great joy and happiness of the sight.
  • Often, when the poet lies on his couch in a vacant or pensive mood, the daffodils flash upon his inward eye, which is the bliss of solitude. Then his heart with pleasure fills, and dances with the daffodils.

Theme of the Poem

The main theme is the joy and healing power of nature. The sight of the golden daffodils filled the poet with happiness at the time, and its memory keeps giving him pleasure and removes his loneliness and sadness later in life. Nature is a source of lasting spiritual wealth.

Key Points

  • The poet compares himself to a lonely cloud and the daffodils to the stars.
  • Wealth in the poem means joy and happiness, not money.
  • The memory of the daffodils removes the poet's pensive mood.

lessons.title: Unit 4 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 4 teaches the tools of poetry: syllables and stress, similes and metaphors, imagery, repetition, personification and alliteration.

Syllables and Stress

A syllable is one beat of a word, and the stress falls on one syllable: po-LIT-i-cal (political, 4 syllables); i-den-ti-fi-CA-tion (identification, 6); in-ter-con-ti-NEN-tal (intercontinental, 6); GRACE-ful (graceful, 2).

Simile and Metaphor

  • A simile compares with like or as: He is as brave as a lion. Her hair is as white as snow.
  • A metaphor says one thing is another: Camel is the ship of the desert. She has a heart of stone.

Imagery, Personification, Repetition and Alliteration

  • Imagery — words that make a picture in the mind: a host of golden daffodils; fluttering and dancing in the breeze; ten thousand at a glance.
  • Personification — giving human qualities to things: The flowers danced in the gentle breeze. The wind whispered through the dry grass.
  • Repetition — using a word again and again for effect: I gazed and gazed at the golden flowers.
  • Alliteration — the same first sound in nearby words: She sells sea-shells on the sea shore. My mother made mango mash.

Key Points

  • A simile uses like or as; a metaphor does not.
  • Personification gives human qualities to non-human things.
  • Alliteration repeats the same first sound.

lessons.title: Road Safety — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
Roads are very busy nowadays, and every day many people face road accidents; some are killed and some are injured or maimed. Road safety is very much up to how we use the roads, so we must learn to use them properly and safely.

Crossing and Riding Safely

  • While crossing a road, use a pedestrian crossing or an overhead bridge whenever one is available. Never dash across a road; if there is no crossing, look carefully at right and left and cross only when it is safe.
  • In a bus, never try to get on or off while it is still moving, and do not fool around — a sudden lurch can knock your head against something hard.
  • On a bicycle, pay attention to the road, do not cycle too far out, obey traffic rules, and keep brakes and lights in order.

Rules for Drivers

  • Traffic rules are designed with safety foremost in mind, for everyone including pedestrians; preference is given to pedestrians and children in crossing the road. Traffic signs warn about accident prone spots.
  • Fasten seat belts: a seat belt secures the persons in a vehicle during a collision or a sudden stop and reduces the risk of death or serious injury.
  • There must be no compromise on the quality of brakes and tyres. Lower your speed near schools, on narrow, hilly and rural roads, and when visibility is poor.
  • Tyre-bursts can be avoided by using good quality tyres, inflating them with the right air pressure, and keeping lights and indicators in proper working condition.

The unit's writing task is a formal letter to the City Mayor requesting a park in the area, because children otherwise play on the dangerous roads and people have no healthy place for recreation.

Key Points

  • Cross at a pedestrian crossing or overhead bridge; never dash across.
  • Seat belts reduce the risk of death or serious injury.
  • Lower speed near schools and on narrow or hilly roads.
  • Good brakes, good tyres and right air pressure prevent accidents.

lessons.title: Unit 5 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 5 teaches anaphoric and cataphoric reference and regular and irregular verbs.

Anaphoric and Cataphoric Reference

A pronoun may refer back to a noun named earlier — this is anaphoric reference: I went out with Kashif. He looked tired. Or it may refer forward to a noun named later — this is cataphoric reference: When he entered the room, Bilal was surprised to see his aunt. If they are late again, the hockey players will be scolded by the captain.

Regular and Irregular Verbs

  • Regular verbs make their past forms with -ed: help → helped, study → studied (y changes to i), invite → invited, attain → attained, walk → walked, kick → kicked.
  • Irregular verbs change in other ways: know → knew → known; come → came → come; give → gave → given; keep → kept; buy → bought; cut → cut; sing → sang → sung.

Key Points

  • Anaphoric reference points back; cataphoric reference points forward.
  • Regular verbs add -ed; irregular verbs must be learnt by heart.

lessons.title: Unity, Faith and Discipline — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
The Muslims of the Subcontinent sacrificed the lives of thousands of men, women and children and abandoned their homes, jobs and businesses in their struggle for a separate homeland, where they could practise the teachings of Islam without fear. The basic cornerstones of Muslim ideology are unity, faith and discipline — these ideals are not new to the Muslims.

Unity

Unity means oneness — a state of being a single whole; it rejects differences or breaking into fragments. The Holy Quran teaches the Muslims to hold fast the connection that binds them to Allah and to refrain from breaking into different creeds. The Muslims stood fast as one body in the movement for the creation of Pakistan and succeeded in achieving their goal; their unity kept their hopes alive against the combined hostilities of the British and the Hindus.

Faith and Discipline

Faith means a firm belief, confidence and trust in Allah. Discipline means a mode of life according to rules; it makes sure that people follow the rules of conduct. During the Pakistan movement the Muslims followed the instructions of their leaders in letter and spirit and performed their individual roles as parts of a well-oiled machine.

The Nation in the 1965 War

During the September 1965 war, the whole Pakistani nation stood up like a solid rock which the enemy could not break through, although the enemy was five times more powerful in men and arms. Soldiers, engineers, doctors, businessmen, poets, artists, students and labourers all worked bravely in their own fields, and there were no crimes during the seventeen days of the war. These principles are most important for students, the future builders of the nation, so that our country may develop rapidly and reach greater achievements.

Key Points

  • Unity, faith and discipline are the cornerstones of Muslim ideology.
  • Unity means oneness; faith means firm trust in Allah; discipline means life according to rules.
  • In 1965 the whole nation stood like a solid rock and defeated a bigger enemy.

lessons.title: Unit 6 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 6 teaches present and past participles, the order of adjectives and quotation marks.

Participles

The present participle ends in -ing: cook → cooking, deliver → delivering, swim → swimming (double the last letter), invite → inviting, announce → announcing. The past participle is the third form of the verb: cooked, delivered, swum, invited, announced. In sentences: He is climbing the mountain (present participle). He has climbed the mountain (past participle). The sun has shone all day.

Order of Adjectives

When several adjectives come together, keep this order: number, opinion, size, age, colour, origin. Correct: We took a ride on an old, blue Chinese bus. I like that really big old red antique tractor. My brother rode a beautiful big black Arabian horse. I'd like three good reasons (number before opinion).

Quotation Marks

Quotation marks enclose the exact words of a speaker: Father said, "I will come to your school tomorrow." In an interrupted quotation, both parts are enclosed: "Students," Mr. Sadullah instructed, "please line up at the door."

Key Points

  • Present participle: verb + -ing; past participle: the third form.
  • Adjective order: size and age come before colour and origin.
  • Quotation marks enclose the speaker's exact words.

lessons.title: Handicrafts of Balochistan — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
Balochistan is famous all over the world for its handicrafts: embroidery and needle-work, embroidered Balochi chapals, caps, purses and belts, hand-woven carpets and wall hangings, marble objects, pottery and ornaments — especially silver ornaments. They are popular for the beauty of their design, the richness of their colour and their economical prices, and they are in great demand at home and abroad.

The Famous Embroidery Styles

  • Kowchik of Dera Bugti — embroidered on shawls and shirts for women.
  • Moshamka of Kalat and Khuzdar — on shawls, cushions, table-cloths and bed-sheets, sometimes with tiny mirror work.
  • Jok of Sibi — made with fine thread of various colours, popular all over the country for the delicacy of its design.
  • The needle-work of Muslimbagh, Gulistan and Zhob — made with open and close stitches, needs the least labour and thread, and is specially selected for bridal dresses and garments for small kids.

The women do this work at home in their spare time after their household work, and it adds to the family income; age is no barrier. The Afghan women also brought new designs and techniques, seen at the handicraft shops in Quetta. These skills are very old and have passed from generation to generation.

Marble and Silver

Crude marble is dug out in the Chaghi district and carried to industrial centres including Hub, where it is made into table-sets, ash-trays, bath-tubs and decoration pieces. Balochi silver ornaments are made completely by hand, without any machine, and are in great demand in national and international jewellery markets. Carpets and ornaments earn foreign exchange for the country, and handicrafts boost up the image of Pakistan at the international level.

Key Points

  • Kowchik is from Dera Bugti; Moshamka from Kalat and Khuzdar; Jok from Sibi.
  • The Muslimbagh–Zhob stitch work needs the least labour and thread.
  • Marble comes from Chaghi; silver ornaments are fully handmade.

lessons.title: Unit 7 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 7 teaches infinitives and infinitive phrases, adjectives formed from nouns and verbs, and parenthesis for numbers and letters.

Full, Bare and Split Infinitives

  • Full infinitive — to + verb: I want to help you. They want to eat mangoes.
  • Bare infinitive — the verb without to, after make, let and modal verbs: He made me leave the room. Let me open the door. I will work harder.
  • Split infinitive — a word comes between to and the verb: We are determined to completely eradicate the diseases.

An infinitive phrase is the infinitive with its words: He wants to buy a car for his family. She sat down to write a letter to her friend.

Adjectives from Nouns and Verbs

  • glory → glorious; efficiency → efficient; pain → painful; defect → defective; vision → visionary.
  • irritate → irritating; depend → dependent; accept → acceptable; act → active; consider → considerable.

Parenthesis for Numbers and Letters

Round brackets enclose numbers or letters in a list: Submit the following items: (1) covering letter (2) photocopies of documents (3) two photographs. The story should include: (a) theme (b) plot (c) characters.

Key Points

  • After make and let, use the bare infinitive (without to).
  • Depend becomes dependent; pain becomes painful.
  • Brackets enclose list numbers (1) and letters (a).

lessons.title: Be Kind — The Poem in Simple Words
lessons.notes_html:
The poem Be Kind by Margaret Courtney teaches us to be kind to every member of our family. Its main theme is love for family members.

Stanza by Stanza

  • Be kind to your father. When you were young, he loved you fondly, caught the first accents that fell from your tongue, and joined in your innocent glee. Now he is old: his locks are intermingled with grey and his footsteps are feeble, once fearless and bold — so be kind to him in his old age.
  • Be kind to your mother. Traces of sorrow may be seen on her brow, yet she is loving and kind, and she prays for her child as long as God gives her breath. Cherish and comfort her now with accents of kindness.
  • Be kind to your brother. Wherever you are, a brother's love shall be an ornament purer and richer by far than pearls from the depths of the sea. If the smile of your love is withdrawn, his heart will have dearth and the flowers of feeling will fade.
  • Be kind to your sister. Not many know the depth of true sisterly love: the wealth of the ocean lies fathoms below the surface that sparkles above, so a sister's deep love must be valued, not judged by appearances.

What Kindness Gives Back

In return for our kindness we get many sweet hours: affection weaves us a garland of flowers more precious than wealth or renown, and our kindness blesses our pathway and crowns it. The impact of kindness is ever-lasting.

Key Points

  • Be kind to father, mother, brother and sister.
  • A brother's love is richer than pearls; a sister's love is deeper than the ocean.
  • The reward of kindness is more precious than wealth or fame.

lessons.title: Unit 8 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 8 teaches the degrees of comparison of adverbs: positive, comparative and superlative.

How the Degrees Are Formed

  • Short adverbs add -er and -est: early → earlier → earliest; fast → fastest; hard → harder → hardest; near → nearer → nearest; late → later → latest; soon → sooner → soonest; loud → louder → loudest.
  • Adverbs ending in -ly take more and most: quietly → more quietly → most quietly; loudly, sweetly, angrily, brightly and carefully follow the same rule.
  • Irregular degrees: well → better → best; badly → worse → worst; little → less → least.

Degrees in Sentences

  • Amjad arrived earlier than Bilal. (comparative)
  • The cheetah is the fastest animal on earth. (superlative)
  • His grandfather is recovering rapidly. (positive)
  • Today I am feeling better than yesterday. (well → better)
  • Silver is less expensive than gold. (little → less)
  • She answered most quickly. (superlative)

Key Points

  • Well becomes better and best; badly becomes worse and worst.
  • Little becomes less and least.
  • -ly adverbs use more and most.

mcqs.why: Adverbs ending in -ly take more and most: quietly → more quietly → most quietly.

lessons.title: Importance of Trees — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
Trees add beauty to the world, and no place of beauty is complete without trees. For the earliest man, travel on land was difficult and dangerous, so he used tree-trunks to travel on the rivers; later, large boats and ships were built of wood.

Wood, Cash and Medicine

  • Wood is used for furniture, boats, doors and window frames, and paper is manufactured from wood. Trees provide raw material for many industries, and good timber is sold for good cash.
  • Malaysia is the largest producer of natural rubber in the world. Pakistan exports apples, mangoes and oranges in large quantities and earns a lot of foreign exchange.
  • The olive tree gives edible oil and medicines; Spain is the largest producer of olive oil in the world, and Pakistan has a suitable climate to grow olive trees over 4.4 million hectares.
  • In medicine, quinine made from the Cinchona tree has controlled malaria, and corks are obtained from the cork-oak.

Trees Protect the Land and the Air

Trees check the force of winds and rain, and their roots bind the soil together, so they prevent landslides and soil erosion in floods. They also purify and regulate the atmosphere and protect animal and bird life.

The Green House Effect

Cutting and burning trees releases ever greater quantities of carbon mono-oxide. These gases make a blanket around the earth which holds in the heat of the sun — the green house effect. The rising temperature will melt the ice near the poles, raise the level of the oceans and submerge some islands. We can ensure a happy and healthy future only by making efforts all over the world to increase the number of trees.

Key Points

  • Trees give timber, fruits, medicines, rubber and foreign exchange.
  • Quinine from the Cinchona tree controls malaria.
  • Roots bind the soil and stop erosion; cutting trees causes the green house effect.

lessons.title: Unit 9 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 9 teaches the semicolon and the first and second conditional sentences.

The Semicolon (;)

A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses: You should stop eating so much food; you will have to go on a diet. Your car needs new brakes; otherwise you may not be able to stop in time. We made too many mistakes; we lost the match.

First Conditional — Real Possibility

Pattern: If + present simple, will + verb. If you work hard, you will succeed. If it rains, I will not go to the playground. If you eat a lot of sweets, you'll gain weight.

Second Conditional — Imaginary Situation

Pattern: If + past simple, would + verb. If I had enough money, I would travel around the world. If I were you, I wouldn't argue with my employer. If he worked hard, he would pass the exams.

To change a first conditional into a second, move both parts one step into the past: If he comes, I will go with him. → If he came, I would go with him.

Key Points

  • First conditional: if + present, will — for real future possibility.
  • Second conditional: if + past, would — for imaginary situations.
  • A semicolon joins two complete, closely related clauses.

lessons.title: Providing First Aid — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
First aid is the assistance given to any person suffering a sudden illness or injury, to preserve life, prevent the condition from worsening and promote recovering. It is temporary and immediate help, and any lay man can be trained to administer it. First aid knowledge ranges from taking care of cuts to dealing with an unconscious person. Burns, bone fractures, wounds and bleeding often require first aid.

The Three Ps — Key Aims of First Aid

  • Preserve life — the most important aim is to save life and minimize the risk of death.
  • Prevent further harm — move the patient away from any cause of harm and apply first aid techniques to stop the condition from worsening.
  • Promote recovering — start the recovering process from the injury or illness, for example by applying a plaster to a small wound.

Stopping Bleeding and Caring for Wounds

  • Minor cuts and scrapes usually stop bleeding on their own. If they do not, apply gentle pressure with a clean cloth or bandage and hold it continuously for 20 to 30 seconds.
  • Do not keep checking whether the bleeding has stopped — this may damage or dislodge the clot that is forming and cause bleeding to resume.
  • If blood spurts or keeps flowing after continuous pressure, take the victim to hospital immediately.
  • Clean the wound (cleaning reduces the risk of infection and tetanus), remove dirt with tweezers if needed, apply a thin layer of antibiotic cream to keep the surface moist, and cover the wound so that bandages keep it clean and keep harmful bacteria out.

The First Aid Box

Every office, factory, home and school should have an accessible first-aid box with: band-aids (plasters) for small wounds; elastic bandages for sprained joints or a sling for a broken arm; gauze and adhesive tape for larger cuts; antiseptic wipes and cotton wool for cleaning wounds; safety pins and tweezers; scissors; latex gloves; and calamine lotion for sunburns and stings.

Key Points

  • The three Ps: preserve life, prevent further harm, promote recovering.
  • Hold gentle pressure for 20 to 30 seconds without checking again and again.
  • Clean, apply antibiotic, and cover every wound.

lessons.title: Unit 10 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 10 teaches proofreading and editing, parenthesis for amounts in numbers, and active and passive voice.

Proofreading and Editing

The book's passage is corrected in four ways: verb tense — They have always treated (not treat) me like a special person; Now that I live (not lived) in England; spelling and punctuation — I don't get to see most of them; subject–verb agreement — She is a lady doctor and has (not have) a very loving nature. Always check tense, spelling, punctuation and agreement when you proofread.

Parenthesis for Amounts

Brackets can repeat an amount in figures after the words: He spent ten thousand rupees (Rs. 10000) on buying clothes. Almost ninety percent (90%) students have qualified. Our school has five hundred students (500).

Active and Passive Voice

  • The peon rings the bell. → The bell is rung by the peon.
  • Graham Bell invented the telephone. → The telephone was invented by Graham Bell.
  • People speak English in many parts of the world. → English is spoken in many parts of the world.
  • English is taught by Mr. Ehsan. → Mr. Ehsan teaches English.
  • They will help the poor. → The poor will be helped by them.

Key Points

  • In the passive voice, the object of the active sentence becomes the subject.
  • Proofreading checks tense, spelling, punctuation and agreement.
  • Brackets can show an amount in figures: (90%).

lessons.title: The Pleasure of Reading Books — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
Reading books provides the highest kind of pleasure. Happy is the man who acquires the habit of reading when he is young: with his beloved books he never feels lonely or bored, and he owns a wealth more precious than gold. It is said, "Reading is to the mind what exercise is to the body."

Pleasure, Poetry and Knowledge

  • Books bring immense joy, enlarge the frontiers of knowledge and widen the outlook of the reader.
  • Good novels and books of imagination give pleasure and amusement; when the brain is weary with serious study, an absorbing story is a healthy recreation, and reading is a nice means to de-stress after a hard day's work.
  • The best poetry gives us noble thoughts and beautiful imaginings clothed in lovely and musical language.

Books — Friends for Life

Books stay with us during the whole life: in babyhood we hear fairy tales, in our teens we swallow exciting suspense novels page after page, and as adults we still find gripping books that absorb us. Books contain grains of wisdom: they give sound moral advice and teach us what should be done and what must not be done. A book also gives us a unique chance to link up with authors who lived in different ages and countries — through reading we hear their voices, thoughts and feelings.

Choosing the Right Books

The blessings of the reading habit are many, provided we choose the right kind of books; the wrong books waste our time and give no benefit. Today the habit of reading is slowly diminishing because more and more people prefer to watch TV or surf on the Internet — but modern equipment cannot replace books, because reading develops our comprehension and grows our vocabulary in a way no screen can.

Key Points

  • Reading is to the mind what exercise is to the body.
  • Books are everlasting friends, from fairy tales to gripping adult books.
  • Choose the right books; wrong books only waste time.

lessons.title: Unit 11 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 11 teaches parenthesis for explanatory material, prepositions, and direct and indirect speech.

Parenthesis — Explanatory Material

Brackets mark off extra, explanatory information inside a sentence: Mr. Ajmal (the fat man) has got a job. Ahmed (my best friend) won the first prize. The book (which I bought yesterday) is very interesting. Our teacher (a kind lady) helps every student.

Prepositions

  • I went to Sibi in 2010. (year)
  • He will meet me on Monday. (day)
  • Come to my home at 3 o'clock. (time)
  • He jumped into the river. (movement)
  • My brother has gone to the library. (direction)

Direct and Indirect Speech

  • Statements: She said, "It is raining heavily." → She said that it was raining heavily. (present tense moves one step back)
  • Questions with if: My friend asked, "Do you read books?" → My friend asked if I read books.
  • Wh-questions: She said to me, "Where do you work?" → She asked me where I worked.
  • Requests and orders: He said to him, "Please wait for me." → He requested him to wait for him. The teacher said, "Open the door." → The teacher ordered (the students) to open the door.
  • Back to direct speech, restore the original words and tenses: He said that he had been to Sibi. → He said, "I have been to Sibi."

Key Points

  • In indirect speech, tenses move one step back and that/if is added.
  • Use in for years, on for days, at for clock time.
  • Brackets hold extra explanatory information.

lessons.title: A Silly Master — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
Qasim built a house in the city because he wanted his son and daughter to be well-educated. His old servant Jamal managed his fields in the village. Jamal was very clever, but Qasim was cleverer: by going round his lands he could tell how much grain his fields would produce and estimate the expected income, so he gave Jamal no chance to deceive him, and earned a lot without doing anything himself.

Naeem, the Silly Master

After Qasim's death, his son Naeem became the master — but Naeem was a simpleton. He never took the trouble to go to the village to inspect the fields, because his father had given him enough money for his personal expenses. When the cotton crop was harvested and sold, Jamal sent a lesser amount than usual. Naeem's mother advised him to go to the village and check if everything was going on well, as his father used to do. Naeem was hesitant — he was used to the comforts of city life — but at last he went and stayed with Jamal.

The Jackals' Trick

  • First night: Sitting by the fireplace in winter, Naeem heard the jackals howling outside. Jamal said they were his master's guests who wanted warm blankets. Naeem gave him a thousand rupees; Jamal pocketed the money, went out, threw some stones, and the jackals ran away.
  • Second night: The jackals came again. Jamal said they were hungry and wanted food, as they were not cold any more. Naeem gave another thousand rupees — pocketed again, and the jackals were scared away with stones.
  • Third night: When Naeem asked what the jackals wanted now, Jamal cleverly replied that they did not want anything — they had simply come to say, "Thank you."

The Lesson of the Story

We should always think before we speak — and before we act. Words and decisions made without thinking cannot be taken back, and a careless master, like Naeem, is deceived again and again by a clever servant.

Key Points

  • Qasim was cleverer than Jamal, so Jamal could not deceive him.
  • Naeem believed Jamal's stories and lost two thousand rupees.
  • Moral: inspect your own work, and think before you speak and act.

lessons.title: Unit 12 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 12 teaches transitive and intransitive verbs.

Transitive Verbs — With an Object

A transitive verb needs an object to complete its meaning. The book's examples: My mother taught me. She read a story yesterday. I wrote a paragraph. The peon rings the bell. He sells pencils.

Intransitive Verbs — Without an Object

An intransitive verb completes its meaning by itself, with no object: He jumped. I laughed. The baby cried. The sun rises in the east. The birds fly in the sky.

Quick test: ask "verb + what?" after the verb. If the sentence answers the question, the verb is transitive (read — what? a story). If there is no answer, it is intransitive (laughed — no object).

Key Points

  • Transitive verbs take an object; intransitive verbs do not.
  • Taught, read, wrote, rings and sells are used transitively in the book.
  • Jumped, laughed, cried, rises and fly are intransitive here.

lessons.title: Try Again — The Poem in Simple Words
lessons.notes_html:
The poem Try Again by William Edward Hickson teaches one lesson in every stanza: if at first you do not succeed, try, try again.

Stanza by Stanza

  • Stanza 1: This is a lesson you should heed: if you do not succeed at first, try again and again.
  • Stanza 2: Then your courage will appear, for if you persevere, you will conquer — never fear — try, try again.
  • Stanza 3: Even if you fail once or twice, keep trying; if you want to prevail at last, try again.
  • Stanza 4: If we strive, it is no disgrace though we do not win the race. What should you do in that case? Try, try again.
  • Stanza 5: If you find your task is hard, keep trying; time will bring you your reward.
  • Stanza 6: All that other folk can do, why — with patience — should not you? Only keep this rule in view: try, try again.

Theme of the Poem

The main idea is determination and persistency: we should never give up. Failure is not a disgrace if we strive honestly; people fear difficult tasks because they fear failure, but perseverance removes fear, and patience is essential because success does not come at once — time brings its reward. Winners never quit, and quitters never win. The unit's essay, Struggle is Key to Success, makes the same point: every successful person has faced failure, but he struggled with patience and courage until he won.

Key Points

  • If at first you don't succeed, try, try again.
  • Failure after honest striving is no disgrace.
  • Patience and perseverance bring the reward in time.

Unit 13 teaches the third conditional and practises asking and telling directions.

The Third Conditional — Imagining the Past Differently

Pattern: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle. It speaks about a past that cannot be changed now: If she had invited him, he would have attended the party. If I hadn't quit college, I would have been a teacher. If you had helped him, he would have won the first prize. If it had snowed yesterday, we all would have enjoyed it. He would have been on time for the interview if he had left the house at eight.

Asking and Telling Directions

Useful phrases from the unit's dialogue: Could you tell me the way to the school, please? Go straight on and keep going until you get to the post office. Then turn left and keep going until you get to the main bazaar. Turn right at the bazaar and the school is on your right.

Key Points

  • Third conditional: if + had done, would have done — for the unreal past.
  • Compare: first conditional (will), second (would), third (would have).
  • Directions use go straight on, turn left/right, until you get to.

mcqs.q: What is the pattern of the third conditional?
options: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle
mcqs.why: Third conditional: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle — it speaks about a past that cannot be changed now.

mcqs.q: 'If she had invited him, he would have attended the party' is:
mcqs.why: It follows if + had invited, would have attended — the third conditional for the unreal past.

mcqs.q: What does the third conditional talk about?
options: A past that cannot be changed now
mcqs.why: The third conditional imagines the past differently — a past that cannot be changed now.

mcqs.q: 'If I hadn't quit college, I would have been a teacher' — this means:
options: I did quit college, so I am not a teacher
mcqs.why: The third conditional speaks of the unreal past: he had quit college, so the result (being a teacher) did not happen.

mcqs.q: Which sentence is a third conditional?
options: If it had snowed yesterday, we all would have enjoyed it.
If it snows, we will enjoy it.
If it snowed, we would enjoy it.
If it snows tomorrow, we enjoy it.
mcqs.why: 'If it had snowed yesterday, we all would have enjoyed it' uses had + past participle with would have — the third conditional.

mcqs.q: Compare the conditionals: the first uses will, the second uses would, and the third uses:
mcqs.why: First conditional (will), second (would), third (would have) — as the key points compare them.

mcqs.q: Which phrase is used for asking directions in the unit?
options: Where is the school situated in the map?
Could you tell me the way to the school, please?
Is the school far or near?
mcqs.why: Useful phrases from the unit's dialogue: 'Could you tell me the way to the school, please?'

mcqs.q: According to the directions, after the post office you should:
options: Turn left and keep going until you get to the main bazaar
mcqs.why: Go straight on until you get to the post office, then turn left and keep going until you get to the main bazaar.

mcqs.q: At the main bazaar, which way do you turn for the school?
options: Turn right at the bazaar; the school is on your right
Turn left; the school is on your left
Go straight; the school is behind you
Turn back; the school is at the start
mcqs.why: Turn right at the bazaar and the school is on your right, according to the unit's directions.

mcqs.q: 'He would have been on time for the interview if he had left the house at eight' is:
mcqs.why: Would have been with if + had left is the third conditional pattern, imagining the past differently.

lessons.title: Revision Notes: Reading Facts from Units 9 to 13
lessons.notes_html:
Facts from Unit 9 — Importance of Trees

The earliest man used tree-trunks to travel on the rivers. Furniture, boats, doors and window frames are made from wood, and paper is manufactured from wood. Malaysia is the largest producer of natural rubber in the world. Trees also serve us commercially: Pakistan exports apples, mangoes and oranges and earns foreign exchange, and Spain is the largest producer of olive oil. Trees are important for a clean environment because they absorb carbon dioxide, give out oxygen, bind the soil and check the green house effect.

Facts from Unit 10 — Providing First Aid

A first-aid box includes band-aids, elastic bandages, gauze and adhesive tape, antiseptic wipes and cotton wool, safety pins and tweezers, scissors, latex gloves and calamine lotion. An antibiotic is applied after the wound is cleaned, in a thin layer, to keep the surface moist. Elastic bandages are kept for wrapping sprained joints or making a sling for a broken arm. We should not keep checking whether bleeding has stopped, because this may damage or dislodge the clot that is forming.

Facts from Units 11 to 13

A book guides us as a friend and a teacher: after reading some books it is easy to understand what should be done and what must not be done, and a book links us with authors of different ages and countries. The poem Try Again teaches that struggle is the key to success and that if we lose, we should try again — the poem is based on perseverance, not freedom.

mcqs.q: What did the earliest man use to travel on the rivers?
mcqs.why: The revision repeats: the earliest man used tree-trunks to travel on the rivers, because travel on land was difficult and dangerous.

mcqs.q: Which country is the largest producer of natural rubber in the world?
mcqs.why: Malaysia is the largest producer of natural rubber in the world.

mcqs.q: Which country is the largest producer of olive oil?
mcqs.why: Spain is the largest producer of olive oil in the world, as the revision facts state.

mcqs.q: Pakistan earns foreign exchange by exporting:
mcqs.why: Trees serve us commercially: Pakistan exports apples, mangoes and oranges and earns foreign exchange.

mcqs.q: Why are trees important for a clean environment?
options: They absorb carbon dioxide, give out oxygen, bind the soil and check the green house effect
mcqs.why: Trees absorb carbon dioxide, give out oxygen, bind the soil and check the green house effect — hence they keep the environment clean.

mcqs.q: What does a first-aid box include?
options: Band-aids, elastic bandages, gauze and adhesive tape, antiseptic wipes and cotton wool, safety pins and tweezers, scissors, latex gloves and calamine lotion
mcqs.why: The revision lists the full contents of a first-aid box, from band-aids and elastic bandages to latex gloves and calamine lotion.

mcqs.q: How is an antibiotic applied?
options: Before cleaning, in a thick layer
After the wound is cleaned, in a thin layer, to keep the surface moist
mcqs.why: An antibiotic is applied after the wound is cleaned, in a thin layer, to keep the surface moist.

mcqs.q: Elastic bandages are kept for:
options: Wrapping sprained joints or making a sling for a broken arm
mcqs.why: Elastic bandages are kept for wrapping sprained joints or making a sling for a broken arm.

mcqs.q: Why should we not keep checking whether bleeding has stopped?
options: It may damage or dislodge the clot that is forming
It makes the patient nervous only
mcqs.why: Checking again and again may damage or dislodge the clot that is forming and cause bleeding to resume.

mcqs.q: The poem Try Again is based on:
mcqs.why: The revision states the poem Try Again teaches that struggle is the key to success and is based on perseverance, not freedom.

lessons.title: Revision Notes: Grammar Facts from Units 9 to 13
lessons.notes_html:
Idioms in Sentences

  • Cry wolf: Do not cry wolf again and again, or nobody will believe you in real danger.
  • See eye to eye: Ali and I see eye to eye on the importance of reading books.
  • Read between the lines: Read between the lines to understand the poet's real message.
  • Time flies: Time flies so fast that the school year is almost over.
  • Go from strength to strength: Since he started working hard, he has gone from strength to strength.

Conditionals — Completing the Sentences

  • First: If he works hard, he will succeed. I will go to Karachi if you come with me.
  • Second: If she laughed, we would be happy. You would be happy if you worked hard.
  • Third: We would have taken our umbrella if it had rained.

Active and Passive Voice

Mother washes dishes. → Dishes are washed by mother. He has finished his work. → His work has been finished by him. The window is opened by Imran. → Imran opens the window. She will accompany her mother. → Her mother will be accompanied by her.

Narration Change

Father said, "I am going to office." → Father said that he was going to office. He said to me, "Can you help me?" → He asked me if I could help him. The teacher said to the student, "Always work hard." → The teacher advised the student to always work hard.

mcqs.q: What does 'cry wolf' mean in a sentence?
options: To call loudly for help once
To raise false alarms again and again, so nobody believes you in real danger
mcqs.why: 'Do not cry wolf again and again, or nobody will believe you in real danger' — cry wolf means raising false alarms.

mcqs.q: 'Ali and I see eye to eye on the importance of reading books' means:
options: Ali and I look at the same book
mcqs.why: See eye to eye means to agree completely — Ali and I see eye to eye on the importance of reading books.

mcqs.q: 'Read between the lines' means:
mcqs.why: Read between the lines to understand the poet's real message — the hidden or implied meaning.

mcqs.q: 'Time flies so fast that the school year is almost over' — 'time flies' means:
mcqs.why: Time flies means time passes very quickly, as the revision sentence shows.

mcqs.q: 'He has gone from strength to strength' means he has:
mcqs.why: Since he started working hard, he has gone from strength to strength — become more and more successful.

mcqs.q: Which sentence is a first conditional?
options: If she laughed, we would be happy.
We would have taken our umbrella if it had rained.
If he worked hard, he succeeds.
If he works hard, he will succeed.
mcqs.why: First conditional: if + present simple, will + verb — 'If he works hard, he will succeed.'

mcqs.q: Which sentence is a second conditional?
options: If she laughed, we would be happy.
If he works hard, he will succeed.
We would have taken our umbrella if it had rained.
I will go to Karachi if you come with me.
mcqs.why: Second conditional: if + past simple, would + verb — 'If she laughed, we would be happy.'

mcqs.q: Which sentence is a third conditional?
options: If he works hard, he will succeed.
We would have taken our umbrella if it had rained.
If she laughed, we would be happy.
You would be happy if you worked hard.
mcqs.why: Third conditional: would have + past participle with if + had + past participle — 'We would have taken our umbrella if it had rained.'

mcqs.q: What is the passive voice of 'Mother washes dishes'?
mcqs.why: Mother washes dishes → Dishes are washed by mother: the object becomes the subject.

mcqs.q: Father said, "I am going to office" becomes:
options: Father said that he is going to office.
Father asked if he was going to office.
Father said to go to office.
Father said that he was going to office.
mcqs.why: In indirect speech the tense moves back: Father said that he was going to office.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Model Essay on First Aid Awareness During Natural Calamities
lessons.notes_html:
Model Essay (from the Revision)

Natural calamities like floods, earthquakes and storms injure thousands of people, and in the first hours after a disaster, doctors and hospitals may not reach the victims. That is why planning and raising awareness about first aid is so important. Every school, office, factory and home should have an accessible first-aid box, and every citizen should be trained in the three Ps: preserve life, prevent further harm and promote recovering. People should learn to stop bleeding with gentle pressure, clean and cover wounds, and deal with burns, fractures and unconscious persons. Through speeches, posters, demonstrations and school training, the masses can learn that a little first-aid knowledge saves lives. If we plan before a calamity and spread this awareness, we can save many lives when disaster strikes.

The revision also asks why trees are important for a clean environment — trees absorb carbon dioxide, give out oxygen, bind the soil, prevent landslides and erosion, and check the green house effect — and for the paraphrase and summary of the poem Try Again, which are given in full in the Unit 13 lessons of these notes.

mcqs.q: Why is first aid awareness important during natural calamities?
options: Doctors reach every place at once
In the first hours after a disaster, doctors and hospitals may not reach the victims
mcqs.why: Natural calamities injure thousands, and in the first hours doctors and hospitals may not reach the victims — so first aid awareness is vital.

mcqs.q: Which places should have an accessible first-aid box, according to the essay?
options: Every school, office, factory and home
mcqs.why: Every school, office, factory and home should have an accessible first-aid box, and every citizen should be trained in the three Ps.

mcqs.q: What are the three Ps named in the essay?
options: Preserve life, prevent further harm and promote recovering
mcqs.why: Every citizen should be trained in the three Ps: preserve life, prevent further harm and promote recovering.

mcqs.q: People should learn to stop bleeding by:
mcqs.why: People should learn to stop bleeding with gentle pressure, clean and cover wounds, and deal with burns, fractures and unconscious persons.

mcqs.q: Which injuries should people learn to deal with, according to the essay?
mcqs.why: The essay lists stopping bleeding, cleaning and covering wounds, and dealing with burns, fractures and unconscious persons.

mcqs.q: Through what means can the masses learn first aid?
options: Speeches, posters, demonstrations and school training
mcqs.why: Through speeches, posters, demonstrations and school training, the masses can learn that a little first-aid knowledge saves lives.

mcqs.q: What is the essay's message about a little first-aid knowledge?
mcqs.why: The masses can learn that a little first-aid knowledge saves lives, says the essay.

mcqs.q: When should we plan for calamities?
mcqs.why: If we plan before a calamity and spread this awareness, we can save many lives when disaster strikes.

mcqs.q: Why are trees important for a clean environment, as the revision asks?
options: They only provide shade and fruit
They absorb carbon dioxide, give out oxygen, bind the soil, prevent landslides and erosion, and check the green house effect
mcqs.why: Trees absorb carbon dioxide, give out oxygen, bind the soil, prevent landslides and erosion, and check the green house effect.

mcqs.q: The revision also asks for the paraphrase and summary of which poem?
mcqs.why: The revision also asks for the paraphrase and summary of the poem Try Again, given in the Unit 13 lessons.
